item.title: GOP nominating speeches
item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
House GOP leadership candidates are lining up colleagues to give nominating speeches ahead of today’s elections.

Rep. Ben Cline of Virginia said he will nominate Texas Rep. August Pfluger for whip this morning. Cline is set to take over the chair of the Republican Study Committee from Pfluger. Rep. Nathaniel Moran will also give a speech for his fellow Texan.

Rep. Carlos Gimenez of Florida said in an interview he will speak on behalf of Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym, who is running for NRCC chair, and Rep. Julie Fedorchak of North Dakota will give a speech for Utah Rep. Blake Moore, who is running unopposed to keep his position as conference vice chairman.

Speaker Mike Johnson said in an interview he will not be speaking on behalf of any candidate.

item.title: RNC members call for delay in congressional leadership elections after midterm losses
item.description: Their public demand for accountability is another sign of the pressure facing Republicans in the aftermath of the bloodbath.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Jim Jordan.

item.dc:creator: By Erin Doherty
item.content:encoded:
Dozens of Republican National Committee members want congressional Republicans to delay their leadership elections by at least 30 days, arguing that the party must reckon with its widespread midterm losses first.

“There is no way to sugarcoat what happened on Election Day. From coast to coast, and in some of the reddest parts of the country, Republicans were humiliated,” the 31 RNC members — from 21 states and two territories — wrote in a letter shared with POLITICO. Now is not the time, they argue, to “accept the status quo” — it’s time “do some serious soul-searching.”

“We ... urge the House and Senate Republican Conferences to postpone leadership elections for at least 30 days to allow for an initial assessment of the November 3 losses, a substantive discussion of what went wrong, and an opportunity for leadership candidates to explain how they intend to address those failures,” the members write.

The House and Senate GOP are both set to hold elections Tuesday to decide their next slate of leaders, with candidate forums scheduled to begin this morning. A handful of senators, including Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), have also called for a delay following last week’s elections.

In the House, Speaker Mike Johnson will not take the top post again, leaving Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan to battle it out. John Thune is expected to be reelected as the No.1 GOP leader in the Senate.

While the elections appear likely to proceed as scheduled, the letter underscores the brewing discontent within the GOP following last week’s wipe out — including even among some of its most loyal members. Democrats won their largest majority in both chambers in decades and the Republican Party has a lot of work to do to resolve its divisions and overcome President Donald Trump’s unpopularity with voters.

“Rushing these elections before examining what happened risks protecting the very leaders whose decisions need to be examined,” the RNC members wrote. “Accountability must come before leadership elections.”

Amy Kremer, Georgia’s national committeeperson and one of the letter’s signatories, also pressed congressional Republicans to show what they intend to accomplish before choosing their next slate of leaders.

“The people who knock on doors, make the calls, and give their hard-earned money are owed more than business as usual. Before leadership asks for another two years in charge, show us what they intend to deliver in the lame-duck session,” she told POLITICO. “What is the plan to pass the SAVE America Act and move pending confirmations? Our voters deserve specifics and results.”

The RNC faces its own leadership fight after last week’s losses. KC Crosbie, the RNC co-chair, wrote in a letter to members last week that she has “decided to run for chair” of the committee, challenging the Trump-picked Joe Gruters. One day later, the president praised Gruters on his Truth Social, and said “I know he will do an incredible job in 2028.”

item.title: Capitol agenda: GOP leaders face a post-rout reckoning
item.description: The House and Senate GOP are poised to hold separate elections Tuesday to decide who will serve as the top Republicans in the next Congress.

media:content.media:title: Senate Republican Leader John Thune speaks with reporters as he departs a briefing on Capitol Hill on Nov. 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Republican leaders are fighting to keep their power on Capitol Hill Tuesday after stunning midterm losses last week.

The House and Senate GOP are poised to hold separate elections Tuesday to decide who will serve as the top Republicans in the next Congress. The winners are expected to immediately start charting a course back to governing relevance after Democrats gained the largest majorities won by any party in decades and voters delivered a firm rebuke of President Donald Trump.

How it’ll go: House Republicans will hold a candidate forum at 9 a.m. to hear from members running for all leadership positions, and a secret ballot will begin at 1:30 p.m.

Senate Republicans will meet at 9 a.m. It’s unclear how long their forum will continue — with some members pushing for a vote to delay the election to give more time for deliberations. But senior Republicans expect that push to fail and to know who will lead the conference by the end of the day.

What to expect: The House elections will pit existing Republican leaders vying to keep their top spots against insurgents who are hoping to capitalize on a desire from some for a clean slate.

Speaker Mike Johnson is bowing out, leaving Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan to battle it out for the No. 1 perch.

Jordan is pledging a fresh look for the House GOP’s top echelon and has swiped at Johnson and Scalise for having too often “operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us.”

Scalise is seeking to fend off the throw-the-bums-out sentiment by drawing on his experience as a fundraiser and a set of personal relationships he has closely tended for years.

Thune appears to be on a path to reelection today as Senate GOP leader, despite calls from a handful of senators, like Sen. Ron Johnson for a delay. One benchmark to watch: Sixteen Republicans voted for a similar delay in 2022, when Mitch McConnell sought his final term as leader.

Thune said Monday Republicans will be given plenty of space to talk through how they are feeling after the midterms. He’s pitching himself as ready to lead the conference amid an uncertain final two years of the Trump administration and a lot of 2028 jockeying.

“The job is not for the faint of heart, for sure,” Thune told POLITICO on Monday. “But I feel like I’ve got something to offer and to contribute ... as we think about now having to chart a slightly new direction.”

What else we’re watching: 

— GOP BUCKS TRUMP ON NVIDIA: Senior Republican lawmakers are considering investigating Nvidia over CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, putting Trump’s strong defense of the tech titan at odds with mounting scrutiny from members of his own party. GOP chairs of the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China committees are asking Huang to appear at a closed-door briefing next week that could lay the groundwork for an investigation into Nvidia. Other Republicans are now calling for Congress or other federal authorities to launch probes into Huang’s conduct and Nvidia’s broader dealings with China, arguing the situation is a serious national security risk.

— PERMITTING DEAL DEBATE LAUNCHES: The lead senators negotiating an energy permitting deal are now promising a “healthy amendment process” after the legislation cleared an initial hurdle Monday. Nearly all Senate Republicans and more than a dozen Democrats voted yesterday to advance the bipartisan permitting reform bill. Several of the Democrats who voted to advance the legislation were still critical of it — with some like Sens. Chuck Schumer and Catherine Cortez Masto pushing for further changes to the bill as the voting process continues.

Mia McCarthy, Jordain Carney, Christine Mui, Ari Hawkins, Gabby Miller, Sophia Cai, Owen Dahlkamp, Katherine Long and Nico Portuondo contributed to this report.

item.title: A blue wave complicates the math in New York’s redistricting push
item.description: State Democrats will need to revisit whether a costly push to allow gerrymandering is still a priority.

media:content.media:title: Voters cast their ballots at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine in New York on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Bill Mahoney
item.content:encoded:
ALBANY, New York — Top New York Democrats still want to redraw the state’s congressional maps before 2028. But after Tuesday’s blue wave, their plans might not be as set in stone as they were a few months ago.

President Donald Trump successfully backed redistricting plans in several red states during his second term. The aggressive push led Democrats to respond with their own tit-for-tat efforts. But redistricting in Republican dominated states did not yield the desired results for the GOP — as evidenced by Tuesday’s blue wave — leading leaders from both parties to rethink their approach.

“It is a matter that will certainly be the subject of serious discussion in the Assembly Democratic conference,” said state Assemblymember Charles Lavine, who carries the legislation that would allow for mid-decade changes to the map. “It’s certainly a possibility — a strong possibility, I would say, but I cannot predict what the conference’s position will be.”

New York has been a prime target for Democrats as they’ve engaged in a national redistricting war. Gerrymandered maps could have helped the party flip four congressional seats this cycle.

But the urgency of acting on such a plan diminished a bit on Tuesday night. Democrats flipped one of those four seats, thanks to Cait Conley’s defeat of Rep. Mike Lawler. And Republican gerrymanders backfired elsewhere in the country, translating into a massive majority for Democrats, even without additional New York pickups.

Democratic New Jersey Gov. Mickie Sherrill, from a neighboring blue state,said after the election she will no longer pursue mid-decade changes.

New York Democrats aren’t going that far — at least not yet. Rep. Joe Morelle, who has been the go-between for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and top Democrats at the state level, said “the principals still remain.”

“That hyperpartisan gerrymandering left New York at a decided disadvantage because we couldn’t do mid-term redistricting,” he said. “I will still advocate for moving ahead, and I think other people will as well.”

Redistricting has never been without risks. State lawmakers approved a constitutional amendment this spring to allow for changes. If they do so again in 2027, it will appear on the ballot as a referendum next November.

That ballot question fight will be costly for both sides, plausibly topping $100 million. And it could provide Republicans with an urgently-needed impetus to show up to the polls — reducing the chances that New York Democrats will carry this year’s momentum into 2027’s local elections and eradicate the GOP bench.

“Opposition to this type of amendment can drive out Republicans and common-sense Democrats,” said Assemblymember-elect Marc Molinaro, a Republican who has previously won local races and a congressional term.

This week’s elections “proved” that gerrymandering can backfire, Molinaro said. “In districts that Republicans in other states drew to their benefit, Republicans were trounced.”

That lesson could indeed make some Democrats a bit more hesitant once the dust settles.

Take a region with three districts that are 60 percent Republican and one that’s 60 percent Democratic. That can be redrawn to have four districts that are each 55 percent Republican. That’s a gain of one GOP seat on paper — but it shrinks the breathing room in the others, creating the possibility that each of the four seats is vulnerable in a wave year.

Detailed results of this year’s congressional races in states with Republican gerrymanders like Florida and Texas will soon provide vivid examples of how such maneuvers can backfire in exactly that fashion. And the math in New York isn’t that different.

The New York maps could allow for a new Democratic-friendly district upstate. Rep. Tim Kennedy received 65% of the vote this year, Rep. Paul Tonko got 64%, and Morelle polled at 63%. Reducing the Democratic margins in a couple of those would allow for either Rep. Claudia Tenney’s seat or the district won by Republican Anthony Constantino to be made bluer — but it could also make the currently safe Democrats vulnerable if the political pendulum swings back in 2028 or 2030.

Another Democratic pickup opportunity is on Long Island, where the party has spent years fantasizing about turning the four congressional districts from a 2-2 map to one with a 3-1 edge.

The party improved a bit in those districts this year. But the margins were far from overwhelming — Democratic nominees received 56.7%, 55.2%, 48.9%, and 48.8% of the vote. There’s room to blend those existing seats into districts that increase the odds in one of the GOP districts — but nowhere near enough to guarantee the costly fight would result in a pick-up, especially in a non-wave year.

There are, to be sure, other advantages to gerrymandering. The party could blend the seat won by Conley with Rep. George Latimer’s dark blue district to make both of them locks in the future.

And there is the prize of GOP Rep. Nicole Malliotakis’ Staten Island seat. She received 56% of the vote this year. Her district, surrounded by a sea of Brooklyn and Manhattan seats where Democrats topped 75%, could easily be chopped up and reconfigured with a dark blue shade.

That’s been the top priority for pro-gerrymandering Democrats all decade — the party unsuccessfully sought to use the courts to force a new Staten Island map just this year. That impulse hasn’t changed.

“Staten Island, the people there basically have no choice,” Morelle said. “They don’t really have a way to impact the people who represent them.”

But the state Legislature will ultimately need to decide whether pick-up opportunities like the Malliotakis seat are still worth a fight that’s likely to drown out everything else in New York next year.

“I am personally supportive,” Lavine said. “But because I am only a legislator and not a ruler, I will work with the majority opinion of my colleagues.”

item.title: Some Democrats want more than a Hakeem Jeffries victory. They want a blowout.
item.description: “We can't have months and months of acrimony,” said Rep.-elect Dan Koh.

media:content.media:title: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill on Nov. 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Hakeem Jeffries’ supporters don’t just want him to win — they want him to win big.

The massive Democratic House victory last week has transformed what might have otherwise been a fraught effort for the sitting minority leader to secure the speaker’s gavel, where a smaller majority could have empowered a tightknit block of hard-left holdouts. Now a broader group is intent on sending a message.

“The people want to see unity,” Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana said in an interview. “They don't want to see fighting. They don't want to see infighting. They want to see the level of togetherness to advance an agenda.”

The good feelings surrounding Democrats’ House gains have quieted the debate about the leadership of the caucus, however large it might be. As counting continues and operatives hold out hope for 260 seats — the largest majority for any party since 1993 — progressive activists continue to call for an alternative to Jeffries.

While no sitting or incoming lawmaker has announced outright opposition, several who ran on populist economic platforms are withholding endorsements.

“I want to see who the other options are and what their agendas are, so that we can make sure that it aligns with the needs of my congressional district,” said Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack of North Carolina.

On Capitol Hill, Jeffries’ allies aren’t fretting about the ultimate outcome — he can afford at least three dozen defections — but his allies are now working to unify Democrats ahead of a nominating vote next week and an official tally on the House floor in early January.

“The American people want us to focus in on issues of affordability,” Rep. Jim McGovern of Massachusetts, the incoming Rules Committee chair, said in an interview. “That's what I heard: affordability, affordability, affordability. So let's get on with the business of electing Hakeem as speaker, and let's focus in on what this election was all about.”

The chaotic past four years of GOP rule are hanging over the vote. Hamstrung by relatively tiny majorities, GOP leaders struggled to keep unruly factions in step — often resulting in dramatic confrontations. In 2023, a group of discontented Republicans voted out a speaker for the first time, putting the deposed Kevin McCarthy into the history books.

Many Democrats said they are intent on setting the tone early that this majority will be functional and productive, not constantly racked by factional warfare.

“I don't believe that we can have the kind of acrimony that we had under Kevin McCarthy and the Republicans,” Rep.-elect Dan Koh of Massachusetts told reporters Sunday. “We need to learn from MAGA. … We need to get to the bottom of [President Donald] Trump's corruption and lower costs for people. We can't have months and months of acrimony.”

Jeffries boasts strong backing around the caucus, with power bases in the Congressional Black Caucus, which is projected to have more than 60 members next term, and the New Democrat Coalition, which is tracking toward more than 140 members. While there is overlap between those two groups and there could be defections, support from these two groups alone already puts Jeffries close to the 218 votes he would need in January.

Plenty of top progressives are endorsing Jeffries, too. Rep. Greg Casar of Texas, the Congressional Progressive Caucus chair, is voting for him, as is the group’s influential former chair, Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, perhaps the best-known face of the party’s leftist wing, is also backing Jeffries and whipped out a whiteboard on a recent livestream to explain to her massive social-media following how the speaker election works.

Not everyone is on board. A handful of new members, many but not all of whom are progressive, reaffirmed this weekend that they are as yet uncommitted to Jeffries.

“I have a lot to consider,” moderate Rep.-elect Zack Mullock of New Jersey said Sunday. “But it'll be an important decision that I'm going to talk to a lot of people who know a lot more than I do.”

Outside critics are hoping the noncommittals mean there’s an opening to block Jeffries’ ascension — or at least win concessions. Some leading progressives are framing the upcoming votes as a chance to resolve, or at least talk through, certain internally divisive issues before Democrats enter the majority.

Rep. Ro Khanna of California cited “Medicare for All” health care policy and the U.S. relationship with Israel as particular flashpoints.

“It’s a healthy process to have that conversation,” he said. “I think we will advance some of those policies that people voted for, and I'm part of those conversations.”

Jeffries said Monday he would be having plenty of personal conversations in the coming days.

“I'm going to work hard to talk to every single member about what we've been able to do together over the last two years, and what the opportunities are for us to do together in the next two years, to deliver upon the dramatic change that the American people so decisively voted for,” he said at a news conference.

The members of the new Congress, both incumbent and incoming, will vote on a speaker nomination next week, which requires only a simple majority of Democrats. The tougher test is on the floor in January, where a speaker must win a majority of all 435 members.

One recent benchmark is the backlash Rep. Nancy Pelosi of California faced after Democrats retook the majority in 2018, in the middle of Trump’s first term. After being elected speaker with zero internal opposition in 2007 and 2009, 32 Democrats opposed her comeback in the caucus vote, and 15 ultimately voted for another candidate or recorded themselves as “present” on the floor — barely allowing her to eke through.

But the caucus largely united behind Pelosi as she subsequently battled with Trump, and Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina — who was No. 3 leader under Pelosi — said it was not important that every Democrat be in lockstep.

“I don't know why everybody thinks you got to be unanimous,” he said. “You can have unity and not be unanimous.”

Mia McCarthy contributed to this report.

item.title: House Republicans could be about to clean their own house
item.description: The minority leader contest between Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise will test just how clean of a slate lawmakers want ahead of 2028.

media:content.media:title: Lisa McClain (left) and Steve Scalise (right) are facing doubts from members who want to move cleanly past Mike Johnson's speakership.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
One week after suffering devastating midterm losses, Republicans in the House will decide just how thoroughly to clean their own house.

While Speaker Mike Johnson is exiting the scene in January, Tuesday’s GOP leadership elections will still pit members of the existing leadership structure against insurgents who are hoping to capitalize on the desire for a clean slate.

“Somebody’s got to get fired,” said Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.), who said he is backing outsiders in the three top races “because we got our butts handed to us.”

At the top of that slate is Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, a 20-year House veteran and a well-known face of the GOP’s hard-right wing who nevertheless has never served in the senior leadership ranks. He is facing off for minority leader against Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the sitting majority leader who has held the party’s No. 2 or No. 3 slot since 2014.

Jordan is pledging a fresh look for the House GOP’s top echelon and has swiped at Johnson and Scalise for having too often “operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us.”

But Scalise is seeking to fend off the throw-the-bums-out sentiment by drawing on his experience as a fundraiser and a set of personal relationships he has closely tended — some for a decade or more. He’s expected to benefit as well from the distrust of Jordan held in some pockets of the conference.

His pitch to members has been relatively simple: that he is battle-tested from one Democratic takeover, in 2018, and is best equipped to do it again.

Rep. Mike Haridopolos of Florida said he saw no “bad options” on the leadership ticket but said he was convinced Scalise knows “how to go from the minority to the majority” and also has long experience going head-to-head with Democrats on the floor.

“I think we need, more than ever, clarity of message and clarity of, this is what our agenda will be,” he said in an interview.

The old-vs.-new dynamic is at play in downballot races, as well. Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota is looking to remain GOP whip, effectively moving from the No. 3 to No. 2 spot in the new Republican minority. He’s up against Rep. August Pfluger, an ambitious Texan who chairs the conservative Republican Study Committee — a well-known steppingstone for leadership aspirants.

Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan is similarly looking to stay as Republican conference chair, which will be the No. 3 post, but faces competition from Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida. They are looking to capitalize on grumbling about McClain’s handling of party messaging.

Stutzman — who is backing Pfluger and Houchin in addition to Jordan — said the scale of the GOP losses argued for complete turnover in the senior party ranks: “There's got to be a change. Look at college football. I mean, if you lose, coaches get fired.”

Several other House Republicans who spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak frankly about the secret-ballot race also said they wanted a fresh start — especially after Johnson, Scalise and Emmer centered the GOP’s case for reelection on a policy bill passed more than a year ago.

“We didn't drive a good strong agenda, and I think Jordan is pointing that out,” one of them said. “He is a very good standard-bearer for conservative policies, and he's quite credible all over the country in advocating for that.”

That’s not to say every Republican’s decision is coming down to old guard vs. new, with some saying in interviews they were planning to split their tickets. Some said they would support Jordan and Emmer, while others also said they were voting for Scalise and Pfluger.

Tuesday’s winners are expected to start charting a course back to governing relevance as Democrats enjoy the largest House majority won by any party in more than 30 years. They will also have to navigate the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency after voters delivered a firm rebuke of his leadership over the past two years.

Trump has not taken sides in the race, nor has Johnson.

"We have two extraordinary guys that are running to lead the conference," the outgoing speaker said Monday. "We'll see how that shakes out."

Neither Jordan or Scalise has telegraphed any plans to separate the House GOP from the unpopular president, and most GOP members said that debate would play out on the presidential campaign trail — not on Capitol Hill.

Instead, they said, they wanted their new leaders to focus on positioning the party for a return to the House majority and clawing back some of the 42-and-counting seats they lost to Democrats this year.

“The point of being in the minority is to get to the majority,” Rep. Nick LaLota of New York, who narrowly eked out a win in his Long Island district and declined to say who he would support.

Others have concluded that what happened last week was simply not House leaders’ fault.

“There are people who are going to blame the losses last week on leadership or bad messaging or whatever,” said Rep. Mike Simpson of Idaho, who is backing the three sitting leaders. “The reality is, there's nothing that we could have done that could have stopped this blue tsunami.”

item.title: Machinists union calls on Schumer to step aside as leader
item.description: The letter comes ahead of the Senate Democrats’ first big meeting to discuss next steps on electing their new majority leader.

media:content.media:title: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) speaks with reporters as he walks to his office at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Will Steakin and Dasha Burns
item.dc:contributor: By Will Steakin and Dasha Burns
item.content:encoded:
A major labor union is telling Sen. Chuck Schumer it’s time to go.

The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers sent the New York lawmaker a letter Monday urging him “not to seek another term” as Senate Democratic leader — making the 600,000-member union the latest voice to join the push for a leadership shakeup after last week’s elections.

“After thoughtful discussions with our IAM Union Executive Council, we believe this is the right moment for a new generation to lead Senate Democrats,” the letter reads.

“This week’s elections sent a clear message: working people are demanding change,” IAM International President Brian Bryant wrote in the letter, which was copied to the full Senate Democratic Caucus and obtained by POLITICO.

The letter adds that the moment “will require fresh ideas, new energy and a new generation of leadership.”

In a statement to POLITICO, Bryant was even more blunt: “The IAM Union is through with any member of leadership, in any political party, who stops one iota short of being a ferocious, unyielding and unbending champion of working people.”

Schumer’s office declined to comment. A Senate Democratic aide, granted anonymity to speak candidly, called the letter "a counterproductive move against ... a longtime IAM ally and a steadfast champion of labor."

In his letter, Bryant thanked Schumer for a decade atop the Senate Democratic Caucus and called him “a trusted friend of organized labor.” But he also urged returning and newly elected Democratic senators to pick a “consensus leader” through “a fair and open process,” and laid out a to-do list for whoever gets the job.

That list includes passing a rail safety bill and the PRO Act, which would make it easier for workers to unionize, as well as restoring bargaining rights for federal workers and reviving enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies Republicans allowed to expire. The Senate Democratic aide noted it the machinists' opposition to Schumer for leader was "particularly puzzling given his longstanding commitment to passing the PRO Act."

The letter lands on the eve of the first full Senate Democratic Caucus meeting since the midterms. That meeting will be where Democrats begin to chart the course for electing their next majority leader, with some now saying it might be time to write a new chapter for party leadership — especially looking ahead to 2028.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.)said Monday night that he still considering a challenge to Schumer, while Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) reiterated she wants to hear Schumer’s vision for how he’d lead the party over the next two years before she pledges him her support.

item.title: Chris Van Hollen not closing the door on Schumer challenge
item.description: The Maryland Democrat is also eyeing a presidential run in 2028.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) speaks during a press conference on newly filed Iran war powers resolutions at the U.S. Capitol, on April 13, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney and Calen Razor
item.dc:contributor: By Jordain Carney and Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen told reporters Monday evening that he’s in “listening mode” about a potential bid for majority leader — and isn't yet ruling out running against Chuck Schumer.

“What I've said from the very beginning is we shouldn't have a coronation,” said Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, adding that he “hasn't shut the door.”

Van Hollen’s comments come as Schumer, the current minority leader, is widely expected to be elected to lead the new Senate majority in January. But some Democrats have held off on saying they would vote for the New York lawmaker, arguing they first want clarity on what the party’s strategy will be for the next two years.

Democrats will meet as a group Tuesday to start talking about their path forward.

Van Hollen met with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) on Monday, after she declined over the weekend to rule out her own leadership ambitions. Slotkin reiterated Monday that she will not vote for a majority leader candidate who cannot articulate a plan, especially for the first 100 days.

“I think a lot of members are calling each other and talking to each other and saying the same thing,” Slotkin said.

Both Van Hollen and Slotkin are viewed as potential presidential contenders. Van Hollen, asked previously about speculation that he could run for leader, had suggested that his focus was on 2028 and making sure Democrats win back the White House.

Schumer may not need these two lawmakers to win his leadership election, however: He only needs a majority of his caucus to support him during a closed-door meeting to be convened in early December.

Plenty of Senate Democrats appear more than happy to vote for Schumer after the party exceeded expectations in last week's midterms. Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said Monday he's one of them.

“I plan to continue to support Schumer just as I have, but I'm also very excited about the new ideas and energy that the new members will bring,” said Blumenthal. “We need them and we need to listen to them and the Senate needs to change the way it operates.”

item.title: Jeffries pushes to restrict China chip exports in defense bill
item.description: The post-election push comes as Nvidia investigates an alleged Chinese spy effort targeting its CEO.

media:content.media:title: Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks with reporters during a news conference in Washington on Monday.

item.dc:creator: By Jalen Beckford and Riley Rogerson
item.dc:contributor: By Jalen Beckford and Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says he’ll push to use the annual defense policy bill to tighten restrictions on advanced chip exports to China, an effort gaining momentum amid the revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.


"There are provisions currently in the Senate version of the NDAA that will restrict chip access to China that I strongly support, and I think we're going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version of the National Defense Authorization,” Jeffries told reporters Monday.

The House Democratic leader’s comments came a day after Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation into Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Jeffries’ backing gives a bipartisan Senate push more support in the House as Democrats prepare to take control of the House and Senate following the party’s strong midterm showing.

The Senate legislation, the AI Overwatch Act, would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China and other countries of concern. Other provisions would help track where exported chips end up and tighten restrictions on sales of the equipment used to make them.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Jim Banks (R-Ind.) also called Monday for Congress to include the AI Overwatch Act in the defense bill, citing reports that Nvidia had secured approval to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to its military.

“NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China’s intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related,” the senators wrote in a statement.

item.title: Westerman bows out of Natural Resources race
item.description: The Arkansas Republican has led the GOP side of the House committee for six years.

media:content.media:title: House Natural Resources Chair Bruce Westerman (R-Ark.) will not seek a waiver to continue leading the committee's Republicans.

item.dc:creator: By Amelia Davidson
item.content:encoded:
House Natural Resources Chair Bruce Westerman will not return to committee leadership next Congress, leaving an open race for the top Republican spot on the panel next year.

Westerman has led Republicans on the Natural Resources Committee for six years and is opting not to seek a waiver to extend his leadership into the next Congress, a GOP aide confirmed to POLITICO. Punchbowl News first reported the development.

Reps. Pete Stauber (R-Minn.) and Paul Gosar (R-Ariz.) have both expressed interest in the ranking member seat.

Westerman had until now been coy about whether he would look to extend his term atop the committee. Over the past six years, the Arkansas Republican — a forester by trade — has pushed land management and permitting reform policies. He led the committee this year in bolstering fossil fuel production, including by lowering royalties for drilling on public lands.

Stauber, who currently chairs the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, would bring a particular focus on mining and critical minerals to committee leadership. Gosar chairs the Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee and has focused on investigating climate nonprofits.

Across the aisle, Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) is on track to take over as committee chair. Huffman wrote to Democratic colleagues last week saying he would make the committee a nexus for Trump administration oversight and would build out a broad environmental agenda.

item.title: Gooden likely misused taxpayer dollars, spent extravagantly on travel, congressional watchdog says
item.description: The House Ethics Committee also has an open inquiry into the Texas Republican.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Lance Gooden (R-Texas) is seen on Capitol Hill in Washington on Oct. 24, 2023.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
Congressional investigators found “substantial reason to believe” Texas Republican Rep. Lance Gooden used taxpayer dollars for personal luxury travel and may have misreported his campaign spending.

The nonpartisan Office of Congressional Conduct’s findings, made public Monday in a report, identified a pattern of "extravagant expenditures” by Gooden that appear to be outside his official duties. The report also highlights that Gooden sought more in reimbursements — $140,000 in 2025 alone — than any other House member.

Gooden is the latest in a line of House members facing ethics allegations this year, with several forced to resign. Midterm polling showed voters citing corruption in Washington as a key reason for souring on the Republican party, although Democratic lawmakers have also faced allegations.

The OCC report was referred to the House Ethics Committee, which is the entity that can discipline members. The Ethics Committee’s investigation remains ongoing.

Gooden in a statement called the report “bogus,” criticized the OCC and called for the House Administration Committee to investigate the office.

"There’s a reason the Senate doesn’t have an OCC—because of insane, bogus referrals like this one,” Gooden said in a statement. “The Ethics Committee will expose this witch hunt, and I’m calling on House Administration to launch an oversight investigation into the OCC’s target selection and record of failed inquiries."

The OCC declined comment.

Gooden also provided a response to OCC from his lawyers.

The OCC said in its report that Gooden and several members of his team did not cooperate with the inquiry.

Gooden, the OCC report says, received over $72,000 in lodging reimbursements from taxpayer money that shows a pattern of brief stays at luxury hotels between $700 and $4,000 per stay. The lawmaker also received more than $58,000 in airfare reimbursements in 2025 — almost exclusively for business or first-class — using taxpayer money.

The report pointed to instances where official travel was booked using the Chase Travel account of Gooden’s wife. House rules prohibit lawmakers and their relatives from benefiting from the Members' Representational Allowance, which is a taxpayer funded budget for each House member’s office.

“Using a relative’s account allows for the accumulation of private rewards and benefits from official funds, which is prohibited by House rules,” the report said.

The OCC also found “several discrepancies” in Federal Election Commission reports submitted by Gooden’s campaign for credit card and travel-related reimbursements from 2025 to 2026.

item.title: Haley Stevens’ odd day back in Washington
item.description: The Michigan Democrat’s office appeared deserted Monday and she was seen voting on the GOP side of the aisle.

media:content.media:title: The locked office of Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) is seen Nov. 9, 2026, the first day back in session after the midterm elections.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson, Katherine Tully-McManus, Mia McCarthy and Kelsey Brugger
item.dc:contributor: By Riley Rogerson, Katherine Tully-McManus, Mia McCarthy and Kelsey Brugger
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Haley Stevens was nowhere to be found Monday afternoon, but the Michigan Democrat was spotted at House votes that evening — in the GOP cloakroom.

Amid questions about whether the embattled lawmaker would return to Washington after endorsing failed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, Stevens was back in town to cast the first votes since September. But rather than huddling with her party, Stevens avoided her Democratic colleagues by camping out with Republicans, according to three people present who were granted anonymity to speak candidly.

The news, first reported by The Washington Sun, prompts new questions about how Stevens might vote on critical year-end legislation between now and when her term ends — and Democrats retake the majority — at the beginning of January. It also comes as her fate in the House Democratic Caucus remains in question as she may have broken the House rules for crossing party lines to endorse Rogers.

Requests for comment emailed to both Stevens’ campaign and congressional office went unanswered Monday, but Stevens saw a mass exodus of staffers last week after she made her 11th-hour endorsement of a Republican candidate in a state viewed as key to flipping the Senate.

The door to her office in Rayburn House Office Building was locked Monday afternoon. No one responded to a reporter’s multiple knocks nor to knocks from a staffer from another office who tried to enter.

A sign reading “please come in” hangs on the locked doors.

The lights appeared to be off inside the office, however, and a peek through the mail slot revealed. Multiple calls Monday to Stevens’ Capitol Hill office went unanswered, sending callers straight to voicemail without a single ring. A message directed constituents to contact the district office in Farmington Hills, Mich.

A call to that office rang, but no one answered. POLITICO left a voicemail asking whether Stevens planned to return to Capitol Hill for votes.

item.title: John Barrasso says Republicans ‘remain united in our purpose’ as he announces whip bid
item.description: The Wyoming senator is seeking another two years as the GOP’s No. 2 Senate leader.

media:content.media:title: Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) looks on during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol on Aug. 4, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming asked his Republican colleagues for support to remain as the No. 2 party leader next year, saying the GOP needs to offer a “clear alternative” to Democrats following its sweeping Election Day losses.

Barrasso, in a letter to colleagues Monday, said Senate Republicans had a “difficult night” last Tuesday and that they “have both an obligation and an opportunity to demonstrate that we heard the unmistakable message voters sent.”

“As the opposition party in the Senate, we must be equally clear about what we stand for and what we will fight against. We need to draw sharp, principled contrast with the left-wing Majority,” Barrasso wrote in the letter to colleagues, a copy of which was obtained by POLITICO.

Barrasso currently serves as Senate GOP whip and is expected to run unopposed for the position in Tuesday’s election. His pitch to his colleagues come as they are openly grappling with how to move forward after losing control of the Senate last week.

Barrasso said in the letter that while “bipartisan accomplishments matter,” that “bipartisanship cannot come at the expense of our principles.”

A group of conservative senators led by Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson is pushing to delay the leadership elections and has requested a conference meeting to discuss the request Tuesday morning. Barring a broader mutiny that few Republicans expect, Sen. John Thune of South Dakota is expected to be reelected as top GOP leader later in the day.

Barrasso didn’t address the calls for a delay in his letter, but he argued that Senate Republicans will be more effective over the next two years if they are united.

“Our effectiveness will depend on our ability to work together, make tough decisions, and communicate openly,” Barrasso said. “Every Senator deserves to be heard. Every concern deserves consideration. We will not agree on everything, but we remain united in our purpose.”

item.title: Murkowski plans to lead Senate Republicans on spending panel
item.description: The Alaska Republican could elevate energy and environment measures as a leader on the powerful committee.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) looks on during a hearing on Capitol Hill on April 22, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Andres Picon
item.content:encoded:
Senator Lisa Murkowski plans to become the ranking member of the Senate Appropriations Committee in the next Congress, an aide said Monday.

The Alaska Republican will seek to replace current Chair Sen. Susan Collins of Maine as the top Republican on the powerful panel after Collins lost her bid for reelection, Joseph Plesha, a spokesperson for Murkowski, told POLITICO.

Murkowski’s ascent could elevate the veteran senator’s biggest legislative priorities —including on energy, the environment and defense — toward the forefront of committee business, though she would not hold the gavel. It would also give a key Trump administration antagonist a new perch from which to scrutinize White House spending moves and potentially restrict its agenda.

Senate Republicans are expected to make final decisions about committee leadership early next year. Murkowski, who is expected to get the ranking member slot as the most senior member of the committee next year, is reportedly facing a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.).

Murkowski has been the top Republican on the Senate Interior-Environment Appropriations Subcommittee for more than 15 years and often touts her bipartisan work on the subcommittee with ranking member Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), who is in line to become chair of the subcommittee. It’s not clear whether she will choose to continue to lead that panel, though she would be entitled to it.

Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) is set to chair the Appropriations Committee in the next Congress. The two senators have a good relationship and are expected to work collaboratively — including on stopping the administration’s attempts to unilaterally withhold congressionally approved funding.

The federal government is currently funded through Dec. 11. Appropriators are expected to punt that deadline into next year, but Democratic efforts to use the spending fight to halt funding for the war against Iran could complicate the effort.

In an interview last week with Alaskan radio station KNOM, Murkowski said Collins’ departure “is going to be putting me in a position of higher leadership on the Appropriations Committee.”

She said she wants to help fix what she said has become “a broken process in the Congress,” while working to “do the job that people have sent us here to do.”

Asked about the concerns she is hearing from constituents, Murkowski named high prices and the impacts of a changing climate.

“People are seeing and coming to fear — coming to fear — the fall and what it may bring, and it’s not just here,” Murkowski said. “We’re seeing weather events in other parts of the state where people are feeling not only a vulnerability but an insecurity in being in their own homes, and what are we doing about it?”

She said she wants to address Alaska’s unique energy challenges and discussed the potential for battery storage, small modular nuclear reactors, wind power and “other renewable sources that are more close to where we are.”

item.title: Freedom Caucus lays out legislative priorities for lame-duck session
item.description: The conservative group is also pushing GOP leaders to not leave Capitol Hill until the list of demands is met.

media:content.media:title: House Freedom Caucus Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) speaks with reporters at the U.S. Capitol on July 16, 2025.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Members of the House Freedom Caucus are out with a wish list of priorities they want GOP leaders to accomplish before the party loses its governing trifecta in January.

“In the two months remaining in the 119th Congress, we have an enormous amount of unfinished business to preserve and protect the Republic from an incoming majority party hell-bent on radically changing it,” the board for the conservative group wrote Monday in a letter to Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune

The goal, members said, was to “deny” Democrats “every legislative leverage point possible” ahead of their takeover of Congress next year.

They added, “Let’s hold the line and finish the work.”

The Freedom Caucus is calling on leaders to push through legislation to “codify” President Donald Trump’s border security policies and strengthen voter ID laws in federal elections. The group also wants a government funding package that holds federal spending at existing levels — or appropriations bills without additional policy provisions.

And members said they wanted Republicans to push ahead with a final party-line package that would focus on modernizing U.S. defense systems and providing "significant tax relief for families” — with $1 trillion in spending reductions to offset it.

“Some of us called for action after our first reconciliation package to continue to move to support the American people,” the group wrote. “Unfortunately, the agenda stalled, and now we will no longer have the majority in the next Congress. We respectfully request that we take action in the next 60 days to protect the citizens we represent.”

In the board’s letter, members demanded “a robust permitting bill,” though did not specify if the Freedom Caucus would support a bipartisan bill brokered with the White House that will get its first procedural vote in the Senate on Monday night. They are also urging the Senate to confirm as many of Trump’s nominees as possible.

The letter also highlighted some priorities where they could get Democratic buy-in. One of those areas is expanding a ban on stock trading to the executive and judicial branches.

“We request that we not leave town until we accomplish these objectives,” the members said.

item.title: Immigration groups want more from congressional Democrats than oversight
item.description: Immigrant rights groups, a lodestar for the Democratic Party’s immigration policies, are looking to play a major role in the party’s policy debates over the next few years.

media:content.media:title: The U.S. Capitol building is seen on Nov. 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Eric Bazail-Eimil
item.content:encoded:
Immigration rights organizations and their allies are pushing Democrats to go well beyond investigating the Trump administration. They want Congress to tackle generational issues such as a pathway to citizenship.

In a letter shared first with POLITICO, a coalition of more than 150 organizations urged lawmakers to “prioritize a bold agenda” on immigration in the next Congress and answer voters’ concerns about the tone and tenor of the Trump administration’s deportation crackdown.

They want oversight investigations probing whether the Department of Homeland Security broke the law in its implementation of a mass deportation push. But they're also looking for Democrats to pursue a pathway to citizenship or permanent legal status for some unauthorized immigrants, a clawback of funds given to immigration agencies via past reconciliation bills, and changes to the way Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection carry out their jobs.

“The harms inflicted on immigrant communities by this administration will echo for generations,” the groups wrote. “Congress has the opportunity now to stand with communities under siege and show the world that accountability and justice are possible.”

The letter shows that immigrant rights groups, once the lodestar for the Democratic Party’s immigration policies, are looking to play a major role in the party’s policy debates over the next few years. And it underscores some of the divisions within the party between progressives, who want to take a much more ambitious swing at current immigration laws, and moderate Democrats, who have pushed for a more limited overhaul of Trump administration policies.

While Trump said he is willing to negotiate with Democrats on immigration policy, including some pathway to status for longtime unauthorized immigrants, Trump’s decision to elevate immigration hard-liner and his deputy chief of staff, Stephen Miller, to the role of White House chief of staff could complicate Democrats’ efforts to get ambitious legislation across the finish line.

item.title: House Democrats plan more prominent placement for Jan. 6 memorial plaque
item.description: Senate Republicans currently have it installed in the Capitol basement.

media:content.media:title: Former Jan. 6 Committee Chair Bennie Thompson shakes hands with former U.S. Capitol Police officer Aquilino Gonell in front of the recently unveiled Jan. 6 plaque at the U.S. Capitol on March 25, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
Democrats intend to find a more prominent location to display a memorial plaque honoring the law enforcement officers who defended the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 — which Republicans currently have relegated to the basement of the building.

Rep. Joe Morelle of New York, the top Democrat on the House Administration Committee, confirmed to POLITICO he plans to facilitate the move when his party retakes the majority in January. And while he is still working out the logistics, the relocation would send a strong message about how Congress remembers a widely traumatic event that remains politically divisive.

The Democratic-controlled Congress passed legislation in 2022 authorizing a plaque to be displayed in the Capitol, in honor of the Capitol Police, D.C. Metropolitan Police and others who “bravely protected and defended this symbol of democracy.” An estimated 250 law enforcement officers were injured that Jan. 6, and five present died in the days that followed, according to a report from the select House committee tasked with investigating the circumstances surrounding the occurrence.

By the time the plaque was ready to be installed, however, Republicans had taken over Congress — and many GOP lawmakers preferred to downplay or ignore the episode implicating President Donald Trump in inciting the riot to protest the results of the 2020 election.

Speaker Mike Johnson told the AP in January that the law authorizing the plaque was “not implementable.” Days later, the Senate voted unanimously on a measure requiring the plaque to be displayed in the Senate.

In March 2026, the plaque was mounted in the basement of the Capitol building’s Senate side in a hallway that looks out over the West Front — where some of the most intense fighting happened on that day. Democrats have continued to insist it be moved so more people can regularly see it.

item.title: Capitol agenda: Jeffries faces big choice on Trump
item.description: Some incoming red-district House freshmen want to see Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries attempt to collaborate with the president, while plenty of others don’t want compromise.

media:content.media:title: Hakeem Jeffries looks on during a press conference in Washington on Nov. 4, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson and Mia McCarthy
item.dc:contributor: By Riley Rogerson and Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Dozens of Democratic House freshmen descended on the Hill this week for new member orientation as their party starts debating how exactly it’ll flex its newfound power.

More than 100 incoming members and prospects — overwhelmingly Democrats, but also new Republicans — flooded the halls of Capitol Hill on Sunday, with vibes landing somewhere between excitement and newbie nervousness.

“I promised my voters that I would come here and get to work right away. So I’m really eager to work with our leadership, find out an agenda for getting affordability, addressing the corruption that’s costing Americans money, and getting to work,” incoming Democrat Rep. Fred Wellman of Missouri told POLITICO.

And while some of the more lighthearted conversations were focused on wanting to get to know Montana’s newest incoming member — i.e. the smoke-jumping Sam Forstag, who Massachusetts’ Dan Koh said he had a gym session with along with Colorado’s Manny Rutinel — the party is already deliberating how to wield the mandate millions of American voters just handed them.

First up this week: the future of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, poised to be speaker next year, told ABC News over the weekend he’s a “hard yes” on impeaching the man leading President Donald Trump’s war effort in Iran.

We’re watching for how many Republicans may join him in that House vote after Democrats pummeled the GOP’s war support in the midterms. Even if the secretary survives the vote — expected by the end of this week — another reckoning is likely to come early next year, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress (more on the impeachment move below).

Jeffries this week is also poised to have many of his first in-person conversations with new members as he grapples with the politically tricky decision of how to handle Trump.

Some incoming red-district freshmen want to see Jeffries attempt to collaborate with the president, while plenty of others don’t want compromise.

Jeffries will have to balance his base’s desire to fight back on what they see as the administration’s excesses with party promises made during the campaign to lower costs ahead of 2028 — or at least be seen trying.

Hard-left Rep.-elect William Lawrence of Michigan said in an interview, “We’ll have to put the ball in the president’s court to see what he does.”

“And I hope that he will sign those bills, but we should push him to do so and make clear that Democrats are here to legislate on behalf of the American people and advance popular policies,” he said.

Read also: Trump says his deportation agenda was ‘too tough,’ repeating interest in a deal with Dems

What else we’re watching: 

— HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT LIKELY, GOP MEMBERS SAY: The House is expected to vote on impeaching Hegseth this week — and depending on post-election attendance — the measure could easily pass. Rep. Thomas Massie is expected to file new articles of impeachment Monday to force a House vote, replacing the measure he filed before the midterms. Massie shared an advance copy with POLITICO. Several House Republicans believe the upcoming Hegseth impeachment measure will pass after Tuesday’s catastrophic losses, with some members hungry to place blame for the party’s defeats. Even if only a few Republicans support the measure, dozens of GOP members who lost their seats could skip votes entirely this week.

— SENATE STARTS PERMITTING VOTE — Senators on Monday hold their first procedural vote on the bipartisan permitting deal reached before the election, but the bill’s fate is anything but clear. Supporters say the lame-duck session represents the last, best opportunity to pass legislation to speed up approvals for energy projects, with little expectation that the next Congress, led by Democrats, will be able to reach an agreement with the Trump administration. But newly-empowered Democrats wary of compromise, opposition from key congressional leaders and tribes and other roadblocks could derail the legislation in the coming weeks. POLITICO outlines the issues that could determine where lawmakers ultimately land on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

Leo Shane III, Meredith Lee Hill and Nico Portuondo contributed to this report.

item.title: ‘Russ Vought’s gonna meet his match’: What Murkowski’s ascension means for the White House
item.description: The Alaska Republican has a record of fighting the White House over funding power, and soon she could lock arms with Democrats in that battle.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) speaks with reporters at the U.S. Capitol on March 24, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes and Katherine Tully-McManus
item.dc:contributor: By Jennifer Scholtes and Katherine Tully-McManus
item.content:encoded:
As President Donald Trump loses one of the biggest GOP critics of his administration with Sen. Susan Collins’ defeat, he’s gaining an increasingly powerful Republican antagonist who could pose a bigger liability for his agenda.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski is next in line to become the top Republican on the Senate Appropriations Committee in early January, when Democrats retake control of the House and Senate and Collins, the current chair, leaves office.

And while the 69-year-old Alaskan would not wield the gavel, the senator has already vowed to “get back to governing in the middle” and is expected to work with both parties to rein in Trump’s moves to wrest spending power away from Congress.

That could include siding with Democrats in continuing to block White House budget director Russ Vought’s efforts to put political appointees in charge of approving grants and preventing Trump from executing another mass cancellation of federal dollars next fall — two Trump administration actions Murkowski has denounced.

“Russ Vought’s gonna meet his match,” said former Republican Rep. Rodney Frelinghuysen, who chaired the House Appropriations Committee for part of Trump’s first term.

“She believes in the process, the power of the purse, and I think she’s going to be a power to be reckoned with. Not that Susan wasn’t. But I’m hugely admiring of Murkowski’s outspokenness,” Frelinghuysen added in an interview. “She’s had quite a lot of opinions on the administration breaking the law.”

Anything Murkowski does to challenge the administration is likely to invite ire from Trump as she weighs whether to run for reelection in 2028, when she will almost certainly face a Republican challenger the president endorses. Trump has already backed a GOP challenger to Murkowski once before, in 2021, while calling the incumbent senator “bad for Alaska.”

Murkowski's office did not make her available for an interview, nor did the White House or the Office of Management and Budget comment on how they would expect to work with Murkowski in her new role.

But if Murkowski stays true to the record she has forged in recent years as a senior appropriator, she could be a valuable partner for Democrats, who are currently anticipating at least a four-seat majority in the Senate. They could pick up two more once votes are fully counted in Mississippi as well as in Murkowski’s own state.

Following Republicans’ staggering electoral losses, a centrist like Murkowski stands to gain more influence on Capitol Hill as a voice more aligned with voters than the cohort of defeated incumbents about to exit Washington.

“She's bigger than the appropriations process, which is great,” Frelinghuysen said. “She's going to be a voice that people are going to be listening to, especially after this election.”

The top Republican slot on the Senate Appropriations Committee is Murkowski’s if she wants it, thanks to the deference to seniority observed by both parties when picking committee leaders. Her spokesperson, Joseph Plesha, said in a statement Monday the senator planned to step into the role. Murkowski also previewed her intentions in an interview with a local Alaska radio station after the election last week, where she said that Collins’ loss “is going to put me in a position of higher leadership” on the panel.

The position could help her reelection prospects, should she choose to run for another six years in 2028.

As the current chair of the panel that funds the Interior Department and the EPA, Murkowski has focused mostly on public lands and environmental issues. But she will have the option next year to take her party’s top seat on the defense spending subcommittee, which will be made vacant by Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell’s retirement.

As one of the top four appropriators in Congress, she also would have a stronger hand to protect programs for rural communities and Native Alaskans, bolster defense investment in her state and influence environmental policies that affect the Alaska’s lucrative oil-and-gas industry.

Citing the benefits of public broadcasting in Alaska, Murkowski voted against Trump’s request last year to claw back more than $9 billion from the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which was then forced to dissolve.

She also accused the president of breaking the law in using the “pocket rescissions” maneuver to unilaterally cancel federal cash, and worked to block Vought’s plan to put political appointees in charge of approving federal grants.

Collins took the same stance on all of those issues. But Murkowski has also been much bolder than her colleague from Maine in bucking Trump and the Republican establishment, including by saying publicly that Vought “disrespects” Congress and has eroded trust on Capitol Hill.

Murkowski cast the lone Senate Republican vote last summer against the party-line bill to fund Trump’s immigration enforcement agencies. She was the only GOP senator to support a committee vote to block the president from diverting $1.4 billion for relocating the FBI headquarters. She was also the sole Republican to join more than 150 congressional Democrats in demanding Vought give back pay to federal workers he furloughed during last year’s government shutdown.

Last month Trump said on social media that Murkowski is "Republicans' Worst Senator, by far” and “a DISGRACE to Alaska and our Country” — a broadside that came after the senator endorsed the Democratic candidate who ended up winning the Alaska gubernatorial contest.

Those kinds of knocks have only reinforced Murkowski’s tendency to speak her mind regardless of the potential blowback, said Bill Hoagland, a former top Senate Budget aide who worked with Murkowski when she was a new senator in the early 2000s. He pointed to Murkowski’s successful write-in campaign in 2010 to hold her Senate seat after losing the Republican primary to a Tea Party candidate.

“She’s a survivor,” Hoagland said.

Murkowski has found ways to make inroads with the Trump administration, despite having a sometimes contentious relationship with the president. She is not afraid to ask for help from his top advisers, including Stephen Miller, who has just been tapped as White House chief of staff.

Last year the senator approached Miller to express gratitude for administration policies that boosted energy production in Alaska — though she also warned the top Trump ally not to hamper those efforts by firing droves of federal workers.

Murkowski said in the local news interview last week that she wants to make real legislative headway over the next two years, rather than spend the entirety of the upcoming Congress slamming the president.

“I hope that the Democrats don’t mess this up,” she said. “I hope that they don’t look at this and say, ‘the next two years … it’s gonna be daily retribution directed at Donald Trump.’”

Murkowski would be working atop the Senate funding panel next year alongside incoming Chair Patty Murray, who is also known for her steely resolve. Jim Dyer, who spent more than 30 years on Capitol Hill as a top GOP appropriations aide, said Murkowski would make “an effective partner” for the Washington Democrat.

“By temperament and by personality, she's a strong woman,” he said. “And I think that's the way she'll want to do business.”

item.title: Hakeem Jeffries has a choice to make: Will he work with Trump?
item.description: The presumptive speaker must manage competing theories of how to engage the president in the next two years.

media:content.media:title: Jeffries has tangled with Trump but said last week Democrats are "ready, willing, and able to find bipartisan common ground."

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump said after Tuesday’s midterm drubbing he wants to “work with” Democrats. Now Hakeem Jeffries has to decide if his party will play ball.

As he prepares to lead a massive House Democratic majority, perhaps the presumptive speaker's toughest call will be how to handle Trump. After years of dismissing and denigrating the president, Jeffries has to weigh varying opinions inside his caucus: Some, including incoming red-district freshmen, want to attempt collaboration, while plenty of others want total war.

Trump is already testing Democrats by appointing Stephen Miller, one of their top administration boogeymen, as his new White House chief of staff — prompting a characteristically fierce reply from Jeffries denouncing Miller as a “dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist” whose “presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor.”

But members close to Jeffries acknowledge he might soon have to strike a different tone as Democrats pledge to make good on their campaign promises to lower costs ahead of 2028 — or at least be seen trying.

Rep. Greg Meeks of New York, a longtime confidant of the Democratic leader, said in an Election Day interview that Jeffries has “always been willing to sit down and talk and to negotiate.”

“It has been the other side that has rejected us and called names … tweeting nasty things and cussing at folks and not being an individual who can respect the office of the presidency,” he continued. “Hakeem Jeffries will be that individual.”

Meeks is not alone in suggesting Jeffries could enter dealmaker mode. It is one of two potential avenues House Democrats are pitching for how he should navigate Trump.

The other, preferred by many progressives, involves Jeffries leading House Democrats in passing bills without compromising with the White House, then daring the president to veto them — matching the aggressive plan by Jeffries and fellow Democrats to use their new subpoena powers to investigate Trump, his administration and his allies.

In the wake of Democrats’ massive midterm victory — which could secure them as many as 260 seats — Jeffries has previewed elements of both strategies.

Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Jeffries said Democrats have “consistently made the point that we are ready, willing, and able to find bipartisan common ground with the other side of the aisle as long as we can bring about meaningful change on the issues that matter, and that begins with decisively addressing the affordability crisis.”

But that doesn’t mean there has been proactive outreach: Jeffries had not spoken with Trump as of Sunday morning, he said in an ABC News interview.

A White House spokesperson, Lauren Bis, said Trump is “willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans” but that if “Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”

Jeffries tangled with Trump repeatedly as minority leader, with the two frequently trading barbs on social media.

During last year’s funding fight, Jeffries showed his willingness to wage war with the administration by refusing to deliver Democratic votes to fund the government without extensions of Affordable Care Act tax credits or an end to mass deportation funding. At one point, Trump posted a video depicting Jeffries in a sombrero — suggesting he was more interested in protecting undocumented Latino immigrants than Americans. Jeffries called the post “racist” and “bigoted.”

Trump has a much less familiar personal relationship with Jeffries than with Sen. Chuck Schumer — Jeffries’ Senate counterpart as Democratic leader and fellow New Yorker.

“I’ve seen Donald Trump work with his opponents. He will find something that he can do, something that he agrees with them on,” said Michael Caputo, a longtime Trump adviser who added that the president “will surprise people with the way he’s going to try to work positively in the present environment.”

But Friday’s move to elevate Miller sent another message — that Trump has no plans to back off that aggressive agenda that Democrats find toxic, to say nothing of his dramatic expansions of executive power to sidestep opposition in Congress.

Jeffries faces inevitable standoffs with the administration over government spending deadlines — including a fight as soon as Dec. 11 over blocking Iran war funding. He will also have to head off a U.S. debt default, predicted to occur some time between next summer and early 2028.

During Nancy Pelosi’s speakership, the House and the Trump administration did work out some agreements, most notably to raise the debt ceiling in July 2019. But deals were otherwise scarce. In 2019, the House passed about 400 bills that died in the Republican-controlled Senate or at the president’s desk.

Jeffries will have a hefty Senate majority to work with, but a former Democratic aide from that period, who like others in this story was granted anonymity to speak candidly, called the dynamic between a Democratic speaker and Trump “a very challenging, nuanced line to walk,” and post-election comments from lawmakers underscored that challenge.

“We need to compromise, but we're not going to compromise our values,” Rep. Greg Stanton of Arizona, a senior member of the centrist New Democrat Coalition, said in an interview last week. “But we are going to have to reach agreement and meet halfway in order to get things done.”

That’s a sentiment shared by several incoming members who won historically Republican districts and now want to deliver affordability wins to campaign on in 2028. Asked about how House Democrats should navigate the Trump relationship, Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke of Wisconsin emphasized a need for collaboration on improving people’s livelihoods.

“People are really struggling here and hanging on by a thread, and I think I really worked to build a broad coalition within my candidacy and my campaign, uniting people of all political stripes to vote for me,” she said in a Thursday interview.

But Democrats have shown there is a limit to their appetite for engagement with Trumpworld.

After the New York Times disclosed over the summer that Jeffries accepted a meeting with Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, to discuss affordability issues, many Democrats were surprised and upset.

But the cozy-up approach has worked for at least one prominent Democratic leader, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has seemingly charmed the president — even while criticizing his administration — and says he will work with Trump to lower costs.

But several progressives are suggesting a different vision of the relationship with Trump and are reluctant to compromise on their ambitious legislative agenda to accommodate the president or other Republicans.

Hard-left Rep.-elect William Lawrence of Michigan said in an interview, “We’ll have to put the ball in the president’s court to see what he does.”

“We should be putting bills on his desk to lower costs and to end the war,” he said. “And I hope that he will sign those bills, but we should push him to do so and make clear that Democrats are here to legislate on behalf of the American people and advance popular policies.”

The likely next head of the Congressional Black Caucus, Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana, proposed a similar approach: “We're going to put things on his desk, and we're going to call him out, and we're going to invite the American people to watch,” he said in a post-election interview. “Sign it or veto it, Mr. President. Show the American people where you really stand.”

But other Democrats say they can only game out their strategy so far. As the Miller pick — and the furious Democratic reaction to it — underscored, Trump’s posture toward governing will influence how Jeffries and his party respond.

“That depends on the president, right?” Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado said Wednesday when asked in an interview about navigating Trump. “We have always said that our job is to protect America, to make Americans' lives better, and that we will always have a discussion about how to do that if they're willing to do it. They're the ones that shut the door.”

Lisa Kashinsky, Megan Messerly, Calen Razor and Kelsey Brugger contributed to this report.

item.title: Sanders warns Democrats about spending too much time investigating Trump
item.description: “We've got to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said.

media:content.media:title: “We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump,” Bernie Sanders said.

item.dc:creator: By Cheyanne M. Daniels
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Bernie Sanders on Sunday applauded the Democrats' midterm victories but warned the incoming majority against spending too much time investigating President Donald Trump.

In an interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” the Vermont progressive said holding the Trump administration “accountable” is important — but addressing affordability must take priority.

“We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump,” Sanders said. “We've got to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives.”

Democrats ran on a message of affordability ahead of the midterms, knocking the Trump administration for sky-high gas and grocery prices, the cost of living and rising healthcare costs. But they also vowed to investigate administration officials; incoming House Oversight Committee leader Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) on Sunday warned that Democrats could investigate everything from pardons Trump made earlier in his second term to Trump allies including Elon Musk and the president’s newly appointed chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Still, Sanders on Sunday said the election was about more than just Americans wanting to tackle the Trump administration’s “corruption and illegal, unconstitutional actions.”

“What I think this election was about, is the American people not only expressing disgust with Trump and his policies, but are demanding real change, no more tinkering around the edges,” said Sanders. “And what the American people are saying: Look, we are working long hours. We're worried about our kids. We can't afford healthcare. We can't afford housing.”

But Sanders, who serves on the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP), also told CNN’s “State of the Union” that he would be “open” to a proposal by Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.) to impeach Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.

“At the very least, I think, he is the most dangerous secretary of the HHS in history and he needs to be held accountable,” said Sanders. “We're going to bring him before the committee, that's for sure, and ask him some tough questions that have not been asked of him previously."

And though Sanders accused Trump of being “erratic,” he added that the president is “a good politician” that Democrats may be able to work with.

“I think, when Trump looks out in the world and he sees millions of people working for starvation wages, he might not be unsympathetic to raising the minimum wage to a living wage,” said Sanders. “He would love, I think, to take credit for doing what every other major country does: guaranteeing healthcare to all people.”

item.title: Rep. Robert Garcia: ‘The days of us not fighting back are over’
item.description: The California Democrat formally announced his bid to chair the Oversight Committee in a letter to colleagues Thursday.
