media:content.media:title: "What we’re not going to do anymore is just take that, take the high road and turn the other cheek,” said Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.).

item.dc:creator: By Cheyanne M. Daniels
item.content:encoded:
The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee vowed Sunday to lead a series of probes into Trump administration officials, telling CNN’s “State of the Union” that Democratic leaders will no longer “take the high road.”

“When Republicans go low, what we’re not going to do anymore is just take that, take the high road and turn the other cheek,” said Rep. Robert Garcia. “The days of us not fighting back are over.”

Following his party’s decisive midterm wins, the California Democrat formally announced his bid to chair the Oversight Committee in a letter to colleagues Thursday.

The bid comes after Garcia warned members of the Trump administration and others to “lawyer up.” On Sunday, he added that even members of the president’s family — such as President Donald Trump’s son, Donald Trump, Jr., and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner — could “absolutely” be subjects of the committee’s investigations.

“They should be expected to answer questions,” Garcia said.

He also indicated that pardons Trump made earlier in his second term could be investigated, as well as donors helping finance the president’s White House ballroom; the operation into the removal of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro; the Iran war; and Trump allies including Elon Musk and the president’s newly appointed chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday accused Garcia and other Democratic leaders of “outright threats” and condemned the promised probes of “basically every member of the Cabinet,” including Miller.

“You have members of Congress who, after Tuesday, have done nothing but threaten everything that's happening in this administration. That is not governing, that is not leading, that is not oversight,” Blanche said in an interview immediately preceding Garcia’s. "That's actually a disappointment. And it's sad.”

Blanche on Sunday appeared to indicate the Justice Department could investigate Democratic members at the behest of Trump, who has called Democratic leaders extortionists and, on multiple occasions, called for them to be jailed.

“What Todd Blanche is doing right now is a threat," said Garcia. "He is threatening our committee. He's trying to stop us from doing real oversight."

item.title: Johnson's meeting request
item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Ron Johnson is sending a letter Monday requesting a conference meeting to discuss the midterm results and a delay in the leadership election.

Johnson has gathered enough signatures to force the meeting under the Senate GOP’s rules and is proposing the gathering for 9 a.m. Tuesday.

“Tuesday’s result was a stunning defeat,” Johnson and his backers write in the letter to Conference Chair Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), a copy of which was obtained by POLITICO. “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice”

Republicans still expect their leadership election to be held Tuesday, where Majority Leader John Thune is so far unopposed to lead the party next year in the minority.

item.title: Chris Murphy released from hospital after stroke
item.description: The Democratic senator will miss “several weeks” of votes as he recovers.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) speaks with reporters at the U.S. Capitol on June 1, 2026. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Chris Murphy announced Friday that he has been released from the hospital after suffering a stroke last week but will miss “several weeks” of Senate votes while he continues to recover.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far,” the Connecticut Democrat said in a statement. “In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today.”

He added that he remains in touch remotely with his staff and colleagues.

Murphy, who was hospitalized last weekend, said Friday that he was “diagnosed with a small bleed in the thalamus region of my brain.” Jose Suarez, the chief of neurosciences critical care at The Johns Hopkins Hospital, said in a separate statement released by Murphy’s office that the senator “experienced a small hemorrhagic stroke.”

“He has shown tremendous progress, and at the current rate of improvement, we expect that he will make a full recovery following rehabilitation,” Suarez added.

Murphy is the latest senator to suffer a stroke in recent years. Sens. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) were both hospitalized for strokes in 2022. Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), at that time a Senate candidate, also had a stroke in 2022 that he later described as near fatal.

item.title: Congressional Progressive Caucus chair lays out strategy to ‘wield our power’
item.description: Rep. Greg Casar insists in a memo that progressives will be power brokers in the massive new Democratic House majority.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, center, and other members of the House Congressional Progressive Caucus speak to reporters on Capitol Hill in Washington, March 5, 2025.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
The head of the Congressional Progressive Caucus said his group will still be power brokers in a massive Democratic majority in a strategy memo previewing plans for next term.

“While some in the press have speculated that a majority of this size undermines our influence within the caucus, they have it exactly backwards,” Rep. Greg Casar of Texas said in the Friday memo obtained by POLITICO. “Big majorities are good for getting big things done. Our goal is not to win a battle against other Democratic caucuses. It is to pass longstanding progressive priorities that bring down costs, root out corruption, and boost wages.”

The CPC will have at least 105 members next term, according to the memo. If Democrats had a narrow majority, progressives — and any other faction in the caucus — could have used their votes as leverage. Now that presumptive speaker Hakeem Jeffries will have as many 30 votes to spare, Democrats broadly are recalibrating their approach next term.

Casar laid out a “three-pronged” strategy for the CPC to "wield our power” in the three-page memo — tackling legislation, oversight and “holding Donald Trump to his word on populist economic policies.”

“Small majorities give corporate special interest groups the ability to block popular populist policies by recruiting a small number of opponents; a big majority gives us the advantage,” he said.

Casar previewed how the CPC can engage with Trump, noting that “one of the few bright spots for bipartisan lawmaking” was a housing bill that banned private equity firms from buying homes. He noted the caucus should push Trump to cap credit card interest rates, lower credit card fees for small businesses and lower prescription drug costs.

“While we oppose [Trump] strongly on the vast majority of fronts, we should send bills to his desk that would lower prices and raise paychecks. If he signs them, good. If he vetoes those bills, that will propel us to a continued Democratic majority and a trifecta where a Democratic president can sign these proposals into law,” he said.

Casar also outlined oversight targets beyond the administration, urging Democrats to specifically investigate corporations that use customer data for “surveillance pricing,” health care companies that are “taking advantage of seniors” through the Medicare Advantage program and artificial intelligence labs who are “putting jobs and lives at risk.”

“By focusing not just on the Trump administration but also on big corporations and billionaires, we will show the American people we are not just anti-Trump but also pro-worker and pro-consumer,” he said.

item.title: Pro-Talarico PAC pulls back curtain on historic investment
item.description: The PAC jumped early and big on immigration messaging.

media:content.media:title: A supporter holds up a hat with an American flag for Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico before Talarico arrives to speak at an election night event in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 3, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Samuel Benson
item.content:encoded:
In January, the leading super political action committee backing James Talarico spotted a problem in the data: Talarico was running behind where he needed to be in Hispanic-heavy South Texas in order to win the March primary.

It didn’t take them long to find a winning message.

A late January poll commissioned by the PAC signaled immense outrage among Texas Democratic voters over ICE’s Minneapolis crackdown. The PAC quickly went up on air with an ad cutting a speech Talarico gave at an anti-ICE rally, before Talarico’s campaign went up with their own immigration spot. According to their data, it helped shore up the South Texas vote and secure Talarico’s primary victory over Rep. Jasmine Crockett. As high-profile ICE incidents spread to other parts of the state throughout the summer and fall, the PAC kept the ad on air. In the end, the ad ran across Texas for 244 straight days, making it their single longest-running spot.

“It really moved voters,” Garry Jones, director of Lone Star Rising PAC, told POLITICO.

Talarico’s historic victory Tuesday night was the result of an extremely favorable national environment, a uniquely capable candidate and campaign, a robust statewide coordinated effort, and significant boosts from outside allies. The previously unreported efforts of the top Talarico-aligned outside super PAC amounted to the largest Democratic independent expenditure in Texas history, the group says.

The PAC, funded in part by Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman, spent $44 million this cycle, boosting Talarico in the primary and helping push him across the finish line in the general election. It outspent the top pro-Ken Paxton PAC, Lone Star Liberty, and put more money into Texas than top Senate Democrats’ top PAC, Senate Majority PAC.

Jones said he was in regular touch with SMP, sharing polling that showed Talarico could win.

“By making the investments early … we were able to create a buffer and show that there was other investment in the state, which I think was really crucial in other groups investing in Texas,” Jones said.

After the primary, Lone Star Rising PAC saw an opening with Paxton-skeptical Republicans, many of whom backed Sen. John Cornyn and were moved by the tens of millions of dollars in anti-Paxton spending in the GOP primary.

“There were times in our polling where self-identified non-MAGA Republicans were splitting 50-50 between James and Paxton,” Jones said.

The PAC isolated the few precincts where Cornyn won or came close to winning during the May runoff — mostly in urban Houston, Dallas, Fort Worth, San Antonio and Austin — and launched a targeted mail and broadcast ad campaign aimed at Republican voters. In one, a Republican former state representative talked about Paxton’s impeachment proceedings; another ad clipped Cornyn saying Paxton is “corrupt” and “unfit for office.”

"Our polling made clear James' message and unique ability to communicate with these voters made these types of numbers possible,” Jones said. “This was our theory. The aggressive program we ran to move traditional Republicans voters to James clearly worked, and the theory we set out with months ago was correct."

Days before the election, Jones said he saw an email come through the PAC’s generic inbox: "I'm so sick and tired of your ads. I want to go vote for Ken Paxton 100 times,” the sender, a Republican, wrote. Jones took it as a sign the ads were breaking through.

Talarico won by 12 percentage points, becoming the first Democrat in nearly four decades to win a Senate race in Texas.

item.title: Nancy Pelosi’s successor headlines the latest round of calls
item.description: Scott Wiener bested his rival in a heated and expensive race that pitted San Francisco’s Democratic factions against each other.

media:content.media:title: State Sen. Scott Wiener attends the VIP reception at SF Pride 2023 Kick Off: "A Night Of Queer Entertainment" at The Castro Theatre on June 2, 2023, in San Francisco.

item.dc:creator: By Gregory Svirnovskiy
item.content:encoded:
California state Sen. Scott Wiener has officially won his bid to replace former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi in Congress, The Associated Press projected Friday afternoon, as Republicans shored up their ranks with victories in three ruby red seats by smaller-than-expected margins.

Wiener bested San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan by 9 percentage points in an expensive, heated Democrat-on-Democrat race that pitted the city’s liberal factions against each other. Chan had the endorsement of Pelosi — as well as Saikat Chakrabarti, who finished third in the June primary. She occupied the more progressive lane.

But it wasn’t enough to compete with Wiener, who spent nearly a decade in the state Senate and raised millions of dollars to win a seat he long coveted. Chan has already conceded to Wiener on Wednesday.

Friday also brought welcome news for the GOP, which saw Rep. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.) reelected to his House seat and Republicans Mark Lamb and Anthony Constantino elected in Arizona and New York, respectively.

Lamb and Constantino were almost felled by the blue wave that saw Democrats take over the House and Senate with massive majorities. Retiring Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-N.Y.) won Constantino’s seat by more than 24 percentage points in 2024.

Constantino — who has spent the time since Election Day publicly feuding with other Empire State Republicans on social media — defeated Democrat Blake Gendebien by fewer than 6,000 votes.

item.title: Launching chair bid, Waters targets crypto, prediction markets, private equity
item.description: The California Democrat laid out a lengthy policy agenda and committee improvements in her bid to lead the House Financial Services panel.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) faces two potential challenges for the House Financial Services Committee gavel.

item.dc:creator: By Jasper Goodman and Katherine Hapgood
item.dc:contributor: By Jasper Goodman and Katherine Hapgood
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Maxine Waters on Friday launched her bid to again lead Democrats on the House Financial Services Committee, vowing to "pursue a bold agenda focused on affordability, accountability, and accessibility," according to a letter to colleagues obtained by POLITICO.

The 88-year-old California lawmaker, who has led Democrats on the panel since 2013, is facing a challenge for the job from Illinois Rep. Sean Casten, 54, who launched a bid to topple her Thursday. Illinois Rep. Bill Foster, 71, is also considering running, though he is currently leaning against it.

Waters laid out an array of details about her potential agenda as chair, writing that she wants to pursue housing efforts "expanding affordable housing programs and reforming mortgage finance," find a way to "permanently and independently" fund the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and "help our community banks by reforming deposit insurance." She also said in the letter she wants to "pass legislation to stop Trump’s crypto corruption, establish tough but fair rules of the road for legitimate crypto ventures, and create safeguards to protect consumers, small businesses, community banks and the financial system."

The five-page letter, which represents the most detailed preview of her agenda yet, vows to "rein in bad private equity actors and bring this unaccountable industry out of the shadows and subject it to oversight and regulation" and "eliminate the junk fees that are nickel-and-diming our constituents, such as overdraft fees, late fees, convenience fees, and over-the-limit fees."

She also pledged to "pass legislation to 'AI proof' our financial system and economy" and "rein in predatory lending and predatory platforms, including prediction markets, so that our constituents keep more of their hard-earned dollars in their pockets."

The letter also seeks to address criticism regarding her approach to running the committee and communication with other members. She wrote that she plans to "convene a meeting with potential Subcommittee chairs and Committee Members to discuss collaboration, ways to empower Subcommittee chairs, and create a plan for moving Member legislation and Subcommittee Chair priorities" and hold "listening sessions" for members.

She also vowed to rename the panel the "Committee on Housing and Financial Services" to "put housing first," eliminate "all paper in hearings and markups," and create new committee leadership positions for more junior members.

Waters touted her record in the letter, writing that she knows "how to strike deals, even with Trump officials."

"At a time when Americans are demanding that Congress deliver results, the Financial Services Committee needs experienced leadership that will address the crushing affordability crisis, expand access to housing, foster a dynamic and fair financial system, and hold the corrupt Trump Administration accountable. I am ready and fired up to lead that charge," she wrote.

item.title: Capitol agenda: Shutdown fight coming sooner than you think
item.description: Though Republicans maintain their majorities until the end of the year, some Democrats — ready to flex their new influence after a midterm blowout — want any year-end spending measure to block cash for the Iran war.

media:content.media:title: House Appropriations Committee Ranking Member Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) speaks with reporters alongside Senate Appropriations Committee Ranking Member Patty Murray (D-Wash.) and other congressional Democrats after a meeting at the U.S. Capitol July 22, 2025.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Democrats have a chance before they take power in January to undercut President Donald Trump’s Iran war checkbook. Not everyone is on board.

Lawmakers will have to pass another funding bill by mid-December to avoid a government shutdown. Though Republicans maintain their majorities until the end of the year, some Democrats — ready to flex their new influence after a midterm blowout — want any year-end spending measure to block cash for the military conflict.

But the move could spark a shutdown fight that extends into the next year and overshadows their new majority and other policy goals.

Democrats will have to weigh the pros and cons of instigating a confrontation they won’t necessarily win.

The top Democratic appropriators, at least, didn’t appear to rule out a fight.

“Democrats will absolutely not fund Trump’s war of choice with Iran that has increased costs on American families and made us less safe,” Rep. Rosa DeLauro said Thursday in a statement to POLITICO.

Senate Appropriations Vice Chair Patty Murray, in a statement, also attributed Democrats’ midterm gains to the unpopularity of the Iran conflict: “The American people just voted overwhelmingly to put an end to this war, and we are going to look at every tool we have available to us to bring this disastrous war to an end.”

The top Democrats in both chambers — Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer — have yet to announce whether they will try to use the moment to limit resources for the war.

Jeffries said in a statement that Democrats will have “a leadership conversation” with DeLauro about the war, “but it is clear from this election that the American people are demanding accountability and an end to the war.”

Schumer said in an interview Thursday he’s working with Murray “to get something done” on government funding before the shutdown deadline, but didn’t forecast whether he’d demand a cutoff of dollars.

The party has been consistent for months in its opposition to the Iran conflict and has so far fought off Trump’s requests for a $1.5 trillion military budget and an emergency war funding package.

Still, triggering a shutdown isn’t a risk all Democrats want to take.

“I don’t know where our leadership is on this one, but I would say that definitely there’s got to be a way to wind this down instead of saying, ‘no funding,’” a House Democratic appropriator, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said in an interview.

Read also: Murkowski anticipates ‘higher leadership’ on Appropriations with Collins exit

What else we’re watching: 

— BLACK DEMOCRATS WANT SOUTHERN INVESTMENT: Black lawmakers are urging national Democrats to invest in the South after a string of stunning wins were powered by a surge in Black voters. Many of these lawmakers, who have previously chided donors for not investing earlier in promising candidates, like Scott Colom in Mississippi and Angie Nixon in Florida, are actively seeking commitments for future cycles. “You cannot reap for which you don’t sow,” said Rep. Troy Carter, who is poised to chair the Congressional Black Caucus next year. Across House races Tuesday, turnout in counties that are at least 60% Black surged 21 points compared to the last midterm in 2022, according to a POLITICO analysis of preliminary returns. That’s more than double the increase in votes cast nationally in counties where the population is less than 20% Black.

— JEFFRIES KNOCKS PERMITTING DEAL: Jeffries on Thursday said the Senate permitting deal “falls short” and raised concerns about the bill’s proposed changes to bedrock environmental laws and protections for tribal sovereignty. “We must once again support the clean energy economy and combat the climate crisis with the fierce urgency of now,” a spokesperson for Jeffries told POLITICO exclusively. “However, the current Senate bill under consideration falls short in several areas, including the manner in which [National Environmental Policy Act] reform is undertaken and the failure to adequately protect tribal sovereignty.” Jeffries’ criticism complicates the bill’s path to passage during the lame-duck session, with a Senate procedural vote on the package scheduled for Monday.

Jennifer Scholtes, Riley Rogerson and Nico Portuondo contributed to this report.
